introduction: The guide remembers the household and companions of Muhammad as the Bábí and Bahá’í writings do: with blessings, with stories, and with long testimonies that recite the fourteen holy names. It begins from a principle of kinship: Salmán the Persian, a stranger, belonged to the family, and a Qurayshite uncle did not. Then come Khadíjih’s steadfastness, the fast of ‘Alí and Fáṭimih when the food was given away, the shepherd and the slave made honourable, the mourning of Fáṭimih, Karbala, and sayings of ‘Alí. Jesus drew the same line about kinship (“whosoever shall do the will of my Father”), and John the Baptist about descent; Paul and James say that the weak and the poor were chosen; the Qur’an prefers Mary above the women of creation. Outsiders are here as well, Gibbon moved by Ḥusayn and Carlyle arguing for Muhammad’s sincerity; and two cautions from the New Testament, on intercession and on repetition, put the questions a reader from another tradition will bring to the litanies.
questions: “Whosoever shall do the will of my Father … the same is my brother.” How do the readings hold together reverence for a family by blood and the principle that Salmán belonged to it?
The sons of honoured companions led the killing at Karbala. What do readings 8, 9 and 24 together say about inherited honour?
The family gives away its food “for love of Him”, wishing “no reward nor thanks”. Why has this small domestic story carried so much weight?
“There is one mediator.” How might someone who prays as reading 37 does explain the practice to someone who holds that verse?
When does a list of names, repeated in prayer after prayer, become “vain repetition”, and what keeps it from that?

outside.why: “Send Thy blessings upon the Lord of Yathrib and Batha, and upon His family.” The prayer obeys a verse: God and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet; O ye who believe, ask blessings on him.

Salman the Persian, a foreigner, was counted of the household; Abú Lahab, a kinsman, was not. Jesus, told that his mother and brethren stand outside: whosoever shall do the will of my Father, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.
Descent alone gives no claim. Think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
Khadíjih, steadfast and thankful in affliction. Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.

The family’s fast, and the food given away three evenings running, is the story commentators attach to this verse: they feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him: we wish for no reward nor thanks from you.
They gave what they themselves needed. Jesus of the widow’s two mites: she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had.
The Prince of Martyrs “like the sun of dawn”. Gibbon, an unbeliever in all such matters, thought the tragic scene of the death of Hosein would awaken the sympathy of the coldest reader.
Twelve Imams, “brilliant stars”. Scripture keeps returning to the number: twelve tribes, twelve apostles, and in John’s city twelve gates.
Uvays was a camel-driver, and is honoured after thirteen centuries. God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
A shepherd and a lowly man, honoured “because they were companions”. The council marvelled at unlearned and ignorant men, and took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
A shepherd, a slave, a porter, a bath attendant. Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith?
The companions gave up their homes to plunder and fled to Medina in poverty. Every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or lands, for my name’s sake, shall receive an hundredfold.
A small band of voluntary exiles crossed to Abyssinia. By faith Abraham went out, not knowing whither he went.
A man excuses himself from danger with a verse: do not cast yourselves into destruction. Jesus on the temple pinnacle answers a text with a text: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
Two poets, one who praised and one who mocked, and the mocker was rewarded. If thine enemy hunger, feed him; be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
Some Prophets had their poets. Saul had his: David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá, recalling the passion plays of his boyhood, calls the drama a great educational power. Aristotle: poetry is a more philosophical and a higher thing than history, for it tends to express the universal.
Fáṭimih the best of women, “except that woman which was born of Mary”. The Qur’an on Mary: God hath chosen thee and made thee pure, and hath preferred thee above the women of creation.
At Ghadír-i-Khumm the Prophet raises ‘Alí before the people. Moses is told to set Joshua before all the congregation and give him a charge in their sight.
Fáṭimih “mourned disconsolate in her abode until she perished”. She weepeth sore in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks; she hath none to comfort her.
Sons of honoured companions led the killing at Karbala. Ye build the sepulchres of the prophets, and your fathers killed them.
A great father’s name did not keep the son. Many are called, but few are chosen. What does this do to the pride of descent that readings 8 and 9 allow to the humble?
They revere ‘Alí and do not recognize the One he pointed to. Ye search the scriptures; and they are they which testify of me; and ye will not come to me.
‘Alí’s saying, “His signs are His proof”. Paul: the invisible things of him are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
All the minds of the world could not describe a single one of His signs. To see a world in a grain of sand, and a heaven in a wild flower.
The pilgrims to Ḥusayn are a caravan to the sacred precinct. Chaucer’s pilgrims ride to a martyr’s shrine too: the holy blissful martyr for to seek.

“Whoso visiteth Husayn in his tomb is as one who hath visited God.” The Gospel has the same grammar of visiting: I was sick, and ye visited me; inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these.
The prayer calls on Moses, Jesus, Fáṭimih and others by their virtues. Hebrews, after its roll of the faithful: seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses.

“I seek intercession through Thy chosen ones.” The pastoral letter: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men. Much of Protestant and of Sunni piety refuses the intercession of holy persons. What does the suppliant here think he is doing?
Blessings on Muhammad, chosen for God’s love. The Qur’an: We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.

“The center of the circle of existence.” Carlyle, addressing Victorian Britain, asked only that Muhammad be seen as a great soul in earnest; the distance between the two estimates is the distance outsiders must travel.

Testimony after testimony recites the same fourteen names. Jesus: when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do. When is the repeating of names remembrance, and when is it what he warns against?
The litany of the chosen souls. Israel has its litany too, a psalm whose every verse ends: for his mercy endureth for ever.
The companions through whom the Cause was established. Of whom the world was not worthy.

shortfall: About half of the readings (32 to 58) are salutations and testimonies from prayers of the Báb that name Muhammad, Fáṭimih and the twelve Imáms in nearly identical words; companions were given to the practice (blessing, litany, intercession) and not to each recital.
